title: ‘The Devil Wears Prada 2’ Is Drawing Tourists to Milan Prompting an 18% Increase in Visitors to the Film’s Locations in Italy’s Fashion Capital
full_text: Aug 14, 2026 3:00am PT ‘The Devil Wears Prada 2’ Is Drawing Tourists to Milan Prompting an 18% Increase in Visitors to the Film’s Locations in Italy’s Fashion Capital By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Oscars: Switzerland Selects ‘Who is Still Alive’ About Palestinians Who Escaped Humanitarian Crisis in Gaza 19 hours ago Oscars: Turkey Submits ‘Like a Limbless Tree’ for International Feature Race 20 hours ago American Film Market Expands With Launch of AFM House, Site of Its Innovation Hub 2 days ago See All Courtesy Everett Collection “ The Devil Wears Prada 2 ” is making a heavenly impact on Milan. Just a few months after the theatrical release in May of the long-awaited sequel to “The Devil Wears Prada” – that was partly shot in Italy’s fashion capital that serves as a glitzy backdrop for the film’s third act – pedestrian traffic from international visitors at the movie’s main Milan locations has risen by 18% compared with the previous period, according to a study by the Cities Analytics platform. Related Stories 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ The sequel to the cult classic starring Meryl Streep , Anne Hathaway , Stanley Tucci and Emily Blunt, which features high-profile local cameos, including Donatella Versace and a live-shot Dolce & Gabbana fashion show, is considered the main driver to the influx of approximately 1.5 million international tourists expected to flock to the center of Milan during the summer quarter. More that 451,000 are expected in August alone, says the study released by the local small businesses association Confcommercio Milano, carried out using the Cities Analytics platform. Popular on Variety Confcommercio Milano chief Marco Barbieri said the study “confirms a structural growth trend in international tourism in central Milan,” since the “Devil Wears Prada 2” release, with foreign visitors increasing “by an average of 28,500 per month.” The main visitors to Milan prompted by the “Devil Wears Prada 2” effect are Americans, followed by French and British, according to the study. As for locations, the most notable rise was recorded between the city’s Largo Cairoli square and Palazzo Clerici, within Milan’s quadrilatero della moda luxury shopping district that features in the film (+24%); followed by Galleria Vittorio Emanuele-Duomo (+17%) where Miranda Priestly has a reflective late-night sequence; the Brera Academy (+14%), where Miranda organises one of the film’s most spectacular events, with strobe lights and sequins amidst the Caravaggios; However the interior of Leonardo da Vinci’s Last Supper Museum was replicated on a soundstage, since the lighting from the production would have damaged the real painting; and via Montenapoleone (+13%) the iconic street featuring the dining spot tucked away in a Renaissance courtyard where Emily (Emily Blunt) has lunch with Donatella Versace, played by the designer herself. After becoming a box office hit following its May 1, 2026 release in the United States (and April 29, 2026 in Italy), reaching $220.6 million in the U.S. and $691.4 million globally on a budget of $100 million, “Devil Wears Prada 2” reached 15.2 million views globally in its first five days of streaming since July 29 on Disney+ and Hulu, marking Disney’s biggest live-action movie premiere since “Deadpool & Wolverine.” Meta Suspends AI Image Feature After Days of Backlash Instagram Unveils ‘More Modern’ New Logo, and People Are Already Making Fun of It Meta AI Can Now Use Your Instagram Photos Without Consent. title: Nigel Farage Documentary ‘Where Does the Money Come From?’ Set at U.K. Broadcaster 5 as Parliamentary Standards Watchdog Reopens Finance Probe
full_text: Aug 14, 2026 2:21am PT Nigel Farage Documentary ‘Where Does the Money Come From?’ Set at U.K. Broadcaster 5 as Parliamentary Standards Watchdog Reopens Finance Probe By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Nigel Farage Documentary ‘Where Does the Money Come From?’ Set at U.K. Broadcaster 5 as Parliamentary Standards Watchdog Reopens Finance Probe 25 minutes ago Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund 2 hours ago Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation 2 hours ago See All Getty Images ITN Productions has set “ Nigel Farage : Where Does the Money Come From?,” a one-hour documentary examining the Reform U.K. leader’s finances, to air on 5 , part of the Paramount Skydance Corporation, on Aug. 22. The documentary comes amid continuing scrutiny of Farage’s finances, following the Parliamentary Standards Commissioner’s investigation into gifts made to him and the Aug. 13 Clacton by-election that the sitting MP triggered by resigning his seat and standing again. Related Stories ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery The documentary will examine the donors, companies and payments that ITN said have reportedly brought Farage more than £2 million ($2.7 million) in outside income since he entered Parliament in 2024, along with earnings from broadcasting, after-dinner speaking and reported property interests. A cast of expert contributors will weigh in on reported payments, donations and gifts tied to two crypto financiers, alongside the parliamentary and media scrutiny of Farage’s finances. Popular on Variety Jeremy Daldry, deputy head of U.K. factual at ITN Productions, said Farage’s political reach has the potential to have a huge impact on the nation, adding that the standards commissioner’s investigation makes it the perfect time to unpack the story. “Topical, reactive documentaries are part of our DNA here at 5, and the questions around Farage’s finances really matter to our viewers,” added Federico Ruiz, commissioning editor at 5. “We dig deep into the publicly available information to examine the facts.” Farage announced on July 7 that he would give up his Clacton seat and stand again, framing the vote as a chance for his own constituents to judge him rather than “the establishment.” His resignation, formalized the next day, froze the standards commissioner’s inquiry into a £5 million ($6.7 million) gift from Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne that Farage had not declared. With the Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens and Restore Britain political parties all boycotting the contest, Farage’s most prominent challenger was Count Binface , a novelty candidate campaigning in a dustbin costume, part of a record field of 34 candidates. Farage won on Aug. 13 with 22,239 votes to Binface’s 9,455, and the standards investigation resumed within hours of his re-election, since such inquiries can only continue while their subject holds a Commons seat. If the commissioner finds Farage breached the MPs’ code of conduct, the case would go to the Committee on Standards, which could recommend sanctions ranging from an apology to a Commons suspension – a suspension of 10 sitting days or more can trigger a recall petition and, if signed by enough constituents, a fresh by-election in the seat. Farage is not the only senior Reform U.K. figure facing scrutiny. Deputy leader Richard Tice is under a separate standards investigation, opened in early August, over an alleged failure to declare a paid-for trip when speaking in a Commons debate. Robert Jenrick, who defected to Reform U.K. earlier this year, has also been referred to the standards commissioner by the Conservatives, while the Electoral Commission and police have separately been investigating donations linked to his 2024 Conservative leadership campaign. ITN Productions is the independent producer within newsmakers ITN, known for premium documentaries responding to major world events, including recent 5 titles “Air India Disaster: The Unanswered Questions” and “The Beckhams’ Billions: How Did They Get So Rich?” “Nigel Farage: Where Does the Money Come From?” is executive produced by Daldry, with Katie Harris and Chris Price-Morgan as producer/directors, Rusen Boztas as production manager and Laura Straker as production coordinator. Post-production was handled in-house at ITN Post. title: ‘Black Mirror’ Director Ally Pankiw Roasts ‘Harry Potter’ TV Series, Claiming She Turned Down Gig: “Say No To Funding Transphobia”
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Top Canadian Screen Bodies & Festivals Urge Government To Stay Strong On Global Streamer Contributions The Harrigans Spiral Out Of Control In ‘MobLand’ Season 2 Trailer Disney+ Signs Content Deal With Gary Neville’s The Overlap To Strike Back Against Netflix’s Football Podcast Play View All August 14, 2026 2:02am Ally Pankiw at a Deadline event and 'Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone' TV series Deadline/Getty, HBO Ally Pankiw certainly won’t be working on HBO ‘s upcoming Harry Potter series. The Black Mirror director shared an Instagram post that appears to show an SMS exchange with her agent in which she emphatically turns down an opportunity to board the series. “I have an instinct on the answer but I feel compelled to ask,” writes the agent. “ Harry Potter ? Hard no?” Pankiw responds, “Absolutely fucking not! lol… (But thank you for asking)”, before the agent writes, “Of course :)… I assumed as much… (And agree).” Related Stories News Julianne Nicholson Was "Concerned" About Reprising 'Mare of Easttown' Role In 'Task' Season 2: "Do I Know Who This Person Is?" News 'House Of The Dragon' Season 3 & 'Life, Larry & The Pursuit Of Unhappiness' Finish As Top Performers For HBO Max The Canadian director, who also has credits for the likes of The Great , shared the post with the caption, “It is simply this easy to say no to funding transphobia,” and added the opportunity was “for directing, not acting… obviously lol”. Watch on Deadline Pankiw’s post drew support from the likes of actor and comedian Vic Michaelis , Welcome to Flatch and Big Mistakes actress Taylor Ortega and Loki , Doctor Who and Sex Education director Kate Herron . The latter wrote in the comments, “They’ve asked me twice and I’ve had to explain my answer is never going to change from a no.” We’ve reached out to HBO for confirmation Pankiw was on its list of directors. Pankiw’s post is a reminder of how the series, Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone , has become toxic in many quarters well before its December launch. This is down to Harry Potter writer and creator J.K. Rowling’s long-held views towards trans people, which have created distance between her and the movie franchise’s stars Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint. Even the likes of the upcoming series stars Nick Frost, John Lithgow, Paapa Essiedu and Bel Powley have openly disagreed with Rowling. They now face regular online criticism for joining the show. While Rowling has occasionally fought back against those who dub her transphobic – even at one point tweeting, “I respect every trans person’s right to live any way that feels authentic and comfortable to them” – she regularly shares anti-trans posts, antagonizes openly trans people and has celebrated a UK high court ruling that women are defined by biological sex. The Harry Potter series is based on Rowling’s blockbuster books. She is an executive producer alongside Neil Blair, Ruth Kenley-Letts of Brontë Film and TV and David Heyman of Heyday Films. Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone , titled the same as the first movie, will debut Christmas Day on HBO and will be available to stream exclusively on HBO Max globally. title: Sarajevo Film Festival Boss Jovan Marjanović on Owning Its Powerful Origin Story: “We Connect This Legacy of War… and Build Bridges”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 14, 2026 2:00am Jovan Marjanović Sarajevo Film Festival Jovan Marjanović is aware just how special the Sarajevo Film Festival is. He would know, having worked for the Bosnian festival since he was just 19. Marjanović is 46 now, and comes into his fifth edition as the event’s sole director with buckets of confidence in what this fest has to offer European cinema. Sarajevo is a film festival born out of war — its first edition, in 1995, took place while the city was still under siege — and that sense of resistance, of using film to empower communities, still sits at the heart of the festival today. Related Stories Movies China's $300M Sleeper Hit 'Dear You' Unveils U.S. Trailer Ahead of September Release TV Gerhard Zeiler to Receive 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award British actress Emily Watson has been tapped to head up the Sarajevo Film Festival jury this year, with the event running Aug. 14-21, alongside director of the European Film Academy Matthijs Wouter Knol, Yorgos Lanthimos’ producer Athina Rachel Tsangari, filmmaker Igor Bezinović and actress Sara Klimoska. Watson will also receive the prestigious Honorary Heart of Sarajevo, also being presented to Asghar Farhadi , Diego Luna and Woody Harrelson at this installment. “Because it is an award tied to the city, it doesn’t have to be specifically about Sarajevo, but [about] representing similar values or understanding the world of cinema,” Marjanović tells The Hollywood Reporter about how the team selects their Honorary Heart recipients ahead of the 32nd edition. The fest continues to spotlight a wealth of regional talent, including competition features from Zvonimir Jurić ( Small Things ), Urša Menart ( Everything That’s Wrong With You ), Kosara Mitić ( 17 ) and Dina Duma ( Skateboarding Is Not For Girls ). They’re still balancing that with a glitzier, Hollywood-skewed lineup that includes Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland with Sandra Hüller (set to open the festival ), as well as Luna’s Ashes and Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Cannes-premiering Minotaur . And, of course, the festival’s rich, cultural history will be honored with the closing-night film, a screening of the Oscar-winning, newly restored No Man’s Land , with Harrelson’s 1997 feature Welcome to Sarajevo also set to screen. Below, Marjanović teases what’s to come from the 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival. He talks about the success of the Open Air Premiere Programs, why the CineLink industry lineup helps to underline the importance of Sarajevo’s place on the festival circuit, and the fascinating origin story that still looms large over everyone passionate about this festival: “[We] realized [the power of] communicating through culture and communicating through cinema with the outside world, because Sarajevo was so closed and besieged. That understanding is, I think, what makes this festival really important.” Jovan, how long have you been in charge? Well, I’ve been with the festival for a very long time. Since I was 19, and I’m 46 now. ( Laughs .) So that’s been pretty much all my life. But I’ve been in charge for the past four years. This will be my fifth edition at the helm alone — there were another two editions before that as a co-director. It’s safe to say you care a lot about this film festival. Oh, absolutely! And I’m not alone. A lot of the team has been with the festival for a long time. But at the same time, we always have young people coming up through the ranks and taking over, and it’s been like that since the very beginning. It was always a close group of friends around the festival. We’re not an institutional body or government-owned body. We’re, let’s say, a non-profit based on an association of citizens. That’s the legal framework. So it’s really up to us, you know? We are our own, and it’s really important to have a group of people who care for what they do and have been nurturing it since day one. [The Sarajevo Film Festival] really came from a difficult place. This festival came [during] war and siege and a complete lack of… everything — what Sarajevo went through in the ’90s. When I say everything, I mean food and electricity. It’s a really specific origin story for a festival, but then [we] realized [the power of] communicating through culture and communicating through cinema with the outside world, because Sarajevo was so closed and besieged. That understanding is, I think, what makes this festival really important. Danis Tanović’s ‘No Man’s Land’ Everett Collection How does the festival continue to honor the history of Sarajevo, the Bosnian War, through its programming? I like to think that it’s in the DNA of the festival first and foremost. Somehow, you see things through that prism and understand the world through that prism and try to take important lessons. On the other side, this year there are two films that are coming back after a couple of decades [away from] the festival. We are closing with No Man’s Land . It’s been 25 years since we showed it last time, and it’s a Bosnian film that won the best international Oscar. But it really was a film that changed a lot of things [for] cinema in Bosnia, and put [the country] on the international stage. That’s the closing film of the festival with [director] Danis Tanović and the team in attendance, so I think it’s going to be very emotional. There’s also Woody Harrelson, who is receiving the Honorary Heart of Sarajevo, and we wanted to show the film that he shot here. So we’re honoring him not just with the Heart, but with the screening of Michael Winterbottom’s Welcome to Sarajevo , a film actually shot back in 1996, just a year after the siege was lifted. Both films [ Welcome to Sarajevo and No Man’s Land ] are actually not present that much on streaming. They’re hard to find, for various reasons… Canal+ in France has restored No Man’s Land fully, so it’s an opportunity to screen the brand new, digital 4K restoration of that film. Welcome to Sarajevo , sadly, did not go through that restoration, but we’re going to screen it in 35mm, which has its own magic to it. Other than that, the festival has programs that are human rights-focused and focused on dealing with the past. The spirit of the festival is really in cooperation. Especially regional cooperation. It connects this legacy of war and division. I think the role of the festival was to build bridges between filmmakers. Is that how you would describe the ethos of a festival like Sarajevo? These mid-tier festivals can have a really important cultural impact, especially in European cinema. What kind of conversations do you want to prompt? It’s a festival that really has a reason to exist. But that’s not enough on its own. There needs to be a clear concept of the festival, and our concept has pretty quickly evolved around filmmakers from our region. We wanted to be geographically focused because of this turbulent history and because of the need to be a bridge between very specific territories [in] the Balkans. It’s a myriad of smaller countries with a lot of smaller languages, with a lot of history, but it’s a powerful mix in the end, and I think the festival serves as a common place for filmmakers and cinemas from many of these countries. We’re also a big festival for the city and for the country, where people want to see the best of cinema from elsewhere — arthouse cinema, conversational pieces, and you want to see them as soon as possible. This is a showcase of the best films to come out this year up until now… And there’s no other festival in the world that shows more films from this part of the world than Sarajevo. You won’t see that many films from this part of the world in Berlin or in Cannes or in Venice. Then they have their home here in a way. We are a premier festival for films coming from this part of the world, and then there’s the whole industry side of things that’s also organized around [that], creating an ecosystem based around cinema from this region. How do you balance those projects with the industry lineup? Some big stars come to Sarajevo, but it’s also a great networking opportunity. True. And that’s one of the key things. It has grown organically, the CineLink Industry Days [program]. We started it some 25 years ago, so the festival and the industry section grew together in a way. The festival was always more audience-oriented. But then, when we introduced the competition sections, which are focused on regional cinema, suddenly those gained industry attention as well. So I think there is the question is of, as you said, balance — finding the equilibrium between the two. And I think once you have built an ecosystem that functions, then [one] feeds into the other. A lot of the execs who come here, they maybe have had films at the festival before, [or] they will have them in the future, and a lot of the projects that are at script stage will end up participating in CineLink to [try] fundraise and promote them. Some of them will go on and premiere elsewhere. Others will premiere with us. It’s a lot of meticulous work. Those CineLink sessions are really wide-ranging… The talks are great. Some speakers I’m really looking forward to hearing. Over the years, there’ve been so many different initiatives that then sprang out of these talks, which is another amazing thing. [They have been] directed either at gender equality or completely business[-focused]. It’s important to be a meeting point, and Sarajevo is really a meeting point. People feel that they can meet each other here. It’s kind of buzzing — the city is not too big, it’s not too small either. So there’s enough space. But at the same time, you can feel the festival everywhere in the city. This atmosphere, I think, adds to people being more open to exploring different futures. So the talks are inspirational in my view. You have a really broad mix of Honorary Heart recipients this year. I’m curious to know how exactly you decide who to honor, and why it’s important to have some high-profile Hollywood names in the list. Well, just looking at the list, there is a thread. The award is called the Heart of Sarajevo, and it really has to do with the city and embracing these people. Emily Watson has been coming to the festival for the past 25 years [or so]. Breaking the Waves was the film that won the second Sarajevo Film Festival before we had the regional focus. She won our hearts back then with that film. And then she kept coming back. She was here, pregnant with her daughter, and now she’s coming with her as a 20-something-year-old! So it’s pretty emotional to welcome her back, and she’s gonna head our jury and dive into the selection of films from this part of the world. She’s going to work fantastically with her fellow jurors. Asghar Farhadi was head of the jury in Sarajevo a few years ago, and when you discuss films with someone like him, you build a connection and an understanding of how we see cinema, what he sees, what we like. That’s another strong bond. I’m saying this in addition to their careers, which are all exceptional. Diego Luna… The people from Mexican and Spanish cinema, from Gael García Bernal to Alfonso Cuarón. Alfonso was actually here for the first Sarajevo Film Festival ever, back in 1995. In the middle of the war, he came to show A Little Princess to the children of Sarajevo. And Y tu mamá también is maybe one of the films that defined the generation of the early 2000s, both for cinema-goers and people making films. Alfonso [is] the leader of that generation, with Diego and Gael… And I already told you about Woody Harrelson. He shot a film here back in 1996 and hasn’t been back since. It’s amazing to welcome him back. So it’s important that these recipients have a special connection to Sarajevo? Well, it just so happens [that way]. That’s not what we award. It really is about the respect for their work in cinema first and foremost. Because it is an award tied to the city, it doesn’t have to be specifically about Sarajevo, but [about] representing similar values or understanding the world of cinema. So we need to be close, maybe without ever meeting each other, but through work and worldviews and world values. That’s the key. I know you can’t show any favoritism, but are there any projects you’re particularly excited about this year, maybe out of competition? Yes. Last year, we opened a new section called Open Air Premieres. This has really grown quickly. We have it at a very prominent venue, a thousand-seater outdoor [theater] with a view of the beautiful Sarajevo City Hall. These films are [typically] something that was missing from the overall mix [or] more popular films from the region [such as No Good Men , Ashes , Minotaur ]. Stuff that’s more audience-driven, that can communicate to a bigger crowd. We [also] gave [the Open Air Premiere selection] a new award this year, the Audience Award, that comes with about 20,000 euros in marketing through Cineplexx, so that’s really exciting. I hope the addition of more popular choices for audiences can complete this regional selection. In our summer screen section, we have a lot of the best films of the year from Berlin, from Cannes, from last year’s Venice Film Festival. In both the Midnight Screenings and Kinoscope, there are a lot of new voices in cinema, a lot of genre-bending stuff. So I’m sure that a lot of the audience will drop in for that. We are opening with Fatherland from Paweł Pawlikowski and I think it’s going to be a great opening. It’s exactly the film that fits the profile of the festival. And No Man’s Land , as I said. There are great films in between that I’m really looking forward to: the Berlinale opener No Good Men , the Afghani film. I think it will resonate with the Bosnian audience very much. Palestine 36 from Annemarie Jacir, also something the audience will want and need to see. Then there’s Minotaur from Andrey Zvyagintsev, which carries a lot of weight in terms of what the story is, the corruption it depicts. I’m really looking forward to the entire Open Air program this year. It’s 3,500 seats and a huge screen and a really special place to see films. The 2026 Sarajevo Film Festival runs Aug. 14-21. THR

title: TV Academy Hall of Fame: Sheila Nevins, Absent Due to COVID, Thanks Dr. Fauci for the Vaccine; Bill Hader Pays Tribute to the ‘South Park’ Creators With a ‘Fish Dick’ Story and More
full_text: Aug 14, 2026 1:16am PT TV Academy Hall of Fame: Sheila Nevins, Absent Due to COVID, Thanks Dr. Fauci for the Vaccine; Bill Hader Pays Tribute to the ‘South Park’ Creators With a ‘Fish Dick’ Story and More By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Variety Editor at Large franklinavenue Latest TV Academy Hall of Fame: Sheila Nevins, Absent Due to COVID, Thanks Dr. Fauci for the Vaccine; Bill Hader Pays Tribute to the ‘South Park’ Creators With a ‘Fish Dick’ Story and More 2 hours ago Warner Bros. Discovery’s Gerhard Zeiler to Recieve Directorate Award at This Year’s International Emmys 13 hours ago How ‘All Her Fault’ Helped Put Peacock on the Map in Scripted Awards Conversations 15 hours ago See All TV Academy Documentary icon Sheila Nevins — who holds the all-time record for most Emmy wins by an individual (31), thanks to her long run as president of HBO Documentary Films — had to skip Thursday night’s Television Academy Hall of Fame event, after being diagnosed with COVID and pneumonia. Instead, Nevins sent her acceptance speech via video, and kicked off her thank-yous with a special shoutout: Dr. Anthony Fauci. “I’d like to thank a bunch of important people,” she said. “First and foremost, Dr. Fauci. Finally, I got tested, and lo and behold, they said — and they were right — ‘you’re lucky you got the vaccine because you’re going to be over this in five to eight days.’ And it’s true. This is the eighth day, and I’m testing negative. Thank you again, Dr. Fauci.” Related Stories ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery Nevins was one of six honorees at the Hall of Fame this year, which also included late “60 Minutes” correspondent Ed Bradley, actor Ted Danson ; “ South Park ” co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and “Hacks” star Jean Smart . The event took place at the JW Marriott L.A. Live in downtown Los Angeles — where the TV Academy is set to kick off its annual Televerse conference on Friday. Popular on Variety After her Fauci reference, Nevins wasn’t done. She also had pointed things to say about several of her co-honorees: In the case of Smart, “it’s really quite astounding. Smart, funny, respect for age, beautiful, and most importantly, after so many seasons, able to earn the same amount of money that the men earn.” In the case of Bradley: “I remember those days at ’60 Minutes’ when people could say what they want to say and do what they wanted to do,” she said. “So thank you, man. You were a great newsman, a great reporter.” She thanked “South Park” creators Parker and Stone “for allowing the oligarchy to be punched through animated characters who don’t seem to matter, when, in fact, they can really say Americans are getting fucked.” In the case of late “60 Minutes” anchor Bradley, who died in 2006, his widow, Patricia Blanchet, accepted the award on his behalf. And toward the end of her speech, she acknowledged the troubling times at CBS News, where Bradley was based all those years on the newsmagazine. “In these most troubling of times, when debates abound about what the very nature of the free press is — and when the viability of this most necessary of public services, such a fundamental pillar of our democracy, is at risk — I miss the special skills that Ed brought to the work,” Blanchet said. “The fierce dedication to uncompromising ethics and journalistic standards, the profound compassion and empathy for the voiceless, the deep humanity peppered with great intellect and curiosity, the decency and civility, the wit and grit. “We could all benefit from his mastery now to come to grips with the daunting challenges we currently face as a nation, and indeed as a world,” she added. “Let us learn from and truly uphold Ed’s exceptional legacy. Let us heed Scott Pelley’s warning that CBS News is on fire, and indeed, so are so many of the institutions upon which we rely to uphold our democracy. Let us pick up Ed’s baton and speak truth to power. Let us walk his walk and better safeguard all that is at risk, that we hold so dear in our sacred democracy.” As CBS News’ Leslie Stahl said in her opening tribute to Bradley, “Ed was that the man you saw on television was exactly the man I knew off camera, and he covered a story with compassion. It was because Ed cared so deeply about the powerless. If he covered a story that filled you with joy, it was because Ed himself was so funny and loved to laugh.” For Parker and Stone, Thursday’s ceremony had a bit of serendipity: It was 29 years to the day that “South Park” premiered on Comedy Central — Aug. 13, 1997. Stone started by thanking his family, “because I’ve missed a few birthdays. And also we got the occasional fatwa and security situations.” Stone noted that it’s really deadlines that drive “South Park.” He said: “Trey and I would never have gotten a single episode of television or episode of ‘South Park’ on television without a deadline. And that for me is what television is about. Something going on the air.” Emmy winner Bill Hader, who had briefly worked on “South Park” (and received an Emmy for that time), gave the award to Parker and Stone — and began by telling the story of how the pitch for a “fish dick” storyline on the show came to be. (That anecdote is probably better to hear in person; see it here .) But Hader also wanted to set the record straight about his time on “South Park”: ‘People say ‘you wrote on the show!’ But, I didn’t. I got paid to laugh and watch all these writers and learn from them and how to tell a story. I would not have been able truly to run my own show without watching these guys. That’s where I learned everything.” Accepting her honor, “Hacks” star Jean Smart pointed out that some of her favorite TV moments growing up were when special broadcasts would return for special annual events — like “Peter Pan” with Mary Martin, “The Wizard of Oz” and Charlie Brown specials. “If you missed it, you missed it,” she said. “You had to wait until next year. But now, children can watch whatever they want, whenever they want, as many times as they want. I often wonder what that’s doing to us as a species, not having to ever wait for things, not having to wait for what we want. But that’s a discussion for another day!” Smart was introduced by “Hacks” creators Paul W. Downs, Lucia Aniello and Jen Statsky. “Jean has proven time and time again that she can be funny, dramatic, sexy, vulnerable and strong,” Downs said. “And on ‘Hacks,’ she showed us she can do all of those things, oftentimes in one scene, and sometimes in a single moment.” When it was Ted Danson’s return, he admitted he was a little shy about accepting the honor. “I have a little trouble with acknowledgment,” Danson said. “My mother, during the height of ‘Cheers,’ was asked what she thought of her son’s success, and she said, ‘Well, of course I’m happy for him, but I’ve always believed in the nobility of quiet failure.’ Seriously! So wish me luck.” Danson also paid his respects to the late Jimmy Burrows, who was one of the creators of “Cheers” with Glen and Les Charles. “He was like my dad in show business,” Danson said. “He guided me, taught me what was funny. When he wasn’t around, the few times he wouldn’t direct and someone else was directing, I literally did not know how to play Sam Malone. Because it was all about making Jimmy laugh.” Danson was presented the award by his wife, Mary Steenburgen, who added, “It’s a funny thing to be asked to introduce someone you’re married to. So many temptations. On the one hand, I know Ted Danson, as all of you do, as the charismatic actor whose career has spanned more than four decades. As the man who can make us laugh one minute and break our hearts with something so earnest the next. But I also know the man who has made me coffee every single morning for 31 years.” For Netflix’s co-CEO Ted Sarandos, he noted that he appreciated the honor since he’ll probably never be in line for a regular Emmy: “I have never created, written, or directed a show, so I’m not going to win an Emmy for that. You saw me [as a guest star] on ‘The Studio.’ Clearly, I’m not going to win an Emmy for acting!” Sarandos then made an impassioned support of television: “It is pretty remarkable that with every step of new technology, people still spend a remarkable amount of time watching television,” he said. “It’s incredibly stable, how much time people spend in front of that screen — whatever that screen they choose — and they are looking for those stories that are professionally made by creators with a capital ‘C.’ Because it taps into something deeply human, which is the desire to be told a great story. And television is the best way to tell great stories.” Sarandos gave a shoutout to the producers who have worked on Netflix shows through the years, particularly the early ones like “Arrested Development” creator Mitch Hurwitz. After “Arrested,” Hurwitz was also behind what Sarandos called his favorite Netflix series of all time, “Lady Dynamite.” Comedian Jerry Seinfeld presented the honor to Sarandos. “It’s so wonderful to be at the Academy of Television to induct Ted Sarandos of Netflix into the Hall of Fame. Even though at the same time, it’s hard for me to believe that I am not the one receiving this first,” he quipped. title: ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Review: A Potentially Involving Story Is Weakened by Airless Dialogue and a Misguided Finale
full_text: Aug 14, 2026 1:12am PT ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Review: A Potentially Involving Story Is Weakened by Airless Dialogue and a Misguided Finale A big man in a small city learns that his nonentity of a son killed a Roma man, but as directed, produced, written and edited by Florin Şerban, the film resists sympathy at every turn. By Jay Weissberg Plus Icon Jay Weissberg Latest ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Review: A Potentially Involving Story Is Weakened by Airless Dialogue and a Misguided Finale 2 hours ago ‘Far From the Trees’ Review: A Richly Contemplative Journey of Physical and Mental Meanderings, Beautifully Combining 4K Digital with Super 16 21 hours ago ‘Wandering Trees’ Review: Iconoclastic Director Salvatore Mereu Tries a Newly Minted Fairyale, but Only Fitfully Finds Magic 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Fantascope Films Florin Şerban’s “You Don’t Belong Here” opens with great promise and finishes with a stupefyingly misguided coda: The lengthy minutes in between are rigorously filmed and sharply observed, but would have benefited enormously if the director wasn’t also the producer, writer and editor. Airless pauses between nearly every line of dialogue and a mostly fixed camera allergic to close-ups sink this potentially intriguing story of an upright surgeon in a small city discovering that his teenage son is a racist milksop who killed a Roma man. The static visuals have a certain pedagogical function indicative of scrupulous honesty — no tricks or cuts will interpose on this supposed truthfulness — but the oddly unnatural spaces between every sentence have an artificiality that undercuts the claim to exacting realism. It’s an odd choice from Şerban, whose Berlinale-award 2010 debut “If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle” had a genuinely lively authenticity. Related Stories ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery Things start auspiciously with Mahler’s 3 rd Symphony accompanying shots of the western city of Reșița, the grand music acting as a counterpoint to the town’s anodyne panorama, suggesting that even in such a nondescript place, something beautiful can exist. That idea is quickly shattered when a stream of masked bike riders armed with baseball bats slap “You Don’t Belong Here” stickers on the cars of the Roma community that they then vandalize. When a man comes out to stop them, he’s beaten to death. Popular on Variety The next morning, Dr. Marius (Adrian Văncică) discovers that some Roma went on a rampage in the hospital morgue, trying to claim the dead man’s body. That same day, the surgeon’s teenage son Ioan (Teodor Butănescu) goes to the school nurse asking to be seen anonymously to check on major bruising he claims to have gotten when he fell off his bike. In a very short time, the story is clearly demarcated, allowing Şerban to focus on character. Marius, approaching 50, is a big doctor in this provincial city, not just a surgeon but the director of the hospital, and a man who prides himself on his directness and honesty. Given how cold he is with most of the people around him, it’s surprising he has a decent bedside manner, but there’s clearly a generational divide between him and junior doctor Tudor (Tudor Vîrgă), who goes out of his way to thank the nursing staff following surgery. For Marius’ friend, police chief Silviu (Alex Conovaru), such solicitude is weak and unmanly. That evening, following a threatening encounter with the dead man’s son (Izdrailă Janir), Marius meets his lover Dana (Cristina Richter), and in a lengthy conversation — more like a monologue à la Nuri Bilge Ceylan — he explains that important men like himself need to crack the whip so others will learn how to behave. “I need to be mean,” he explains, before then revealing his insecurities: “What if I’m not as great as I think I am?” He knows he’s a just person, but what if that’s all? The scene is the only one with some honest introspection and also one of the few times when Marius shows any vulnerability, though the truth is, he’s largely dead inside despite later declarations that his son is his entire world. Had Şerban shown even an iota of that father-son love, the film could have professed some kind of emotional core, but what’s seen on screen are people devoid of affection, and only when Marius’s hardened exterior crumbles on learning that Ioan is suspected of murder does the viewer extend begrudging sympathy to the man. (Though when he admits to not feeling love for Dana, that sympathy goes down another notch.) The problem isn’t the characterization, since the surgeon is extremely well drawn and Văncică’s performance picks up on both the overall inner emptiness and the yearning for something more. What really hampers “You Don’t Belong Here” is the frigid mise-en-scène . Every scene feels inert, and for reasons best known to Şerban, Liviu Mãrghidan’s camera keeps a distance from the characters, making us cold voyeurs unable to get near anyone. At least we regularly see Văncică’s face, unlike Butănescu’s, shot obliquely or in shadow, his perpetual downcast posture making him nothing more than an empty cypher, a babyish teen destined to disappoint any parent. Equally unclear is why every line of dialogue has to have a pause before the next character responds; it’s just one of several directorial and script choices, like the truly unfortunate ending, that will leave audiences wondering how much better the story could have been had a producer and editor cracked the whip that Marius boasts about. ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Review: A Potentially Involving Story Is Weakened by Airless Dialogue and a Misguided Finale Reviewed at Locarno Film Festival (International Competition), Aug. 8, 2026 (Also in Sarajevo Film Festival.) Running time: 154 MIN. (Original title: ‘Nu e locul tau aici’) Production: (Romania). A Fantascope Films production in co-production with Scharf Film Production, Avanpost, Earlybird, Adrian Văncică, Asociaţia Art-Act 27, Școala de Film. (World sales: REASON8, London). Producer: Florin Şerban. Co-producers: Ruxandra Flonta, Carmen Rizac, Vlad Rădulescu, Marius Leftărache, Sebastian Plămădeală, Adrian Văncică. Executive producer: Minodora Şerban. Crew: Director, screenplay, editor: Florin Şerban. Camera: Liviu Mãrghidan. Music: Marius Leftărache, Nikita Dembinski. With: Adrian Văncică, Teodor Butănescu, Cristina Richter, Alex Conovaru, Izdrailă Janir, Adriana Neagoe, Tudor Vîrgă, Emil Boroghină. title: Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund
full_text: Aug 14, 2026 12:38am PT Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund 2 hours ago Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation 3 hours ago COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago See All Asian Cinema Fund The Busan International Film Festival ‘s Asian Cinema Fund (ACF) has selected three international co-productions for its 2026 Co-Production Support Fund, backing films from directors Fukada Koji , Jakrawal Nilthamrong and Boo Junfeng with a combined KRW140 million ($100,000) in production funding. The three projects – “Grateful,” “Rhizome” and “Trinity” – were chosen from 15 submissions following a two-round process of materials review and interviews, the ACF said. The lineup marks a threefold jump from last year’s single recipient, and together the films span 13 countries, including Korea, across majority and minority production roles. Related Stories 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ Fukada Koji directs “Grateful,” a Korea-Japan co-production in which Korea holds majority status and Japan participates as the minority partner. Song Dae-chan and Kameda Yuko produce. The project received KRW60 million ($42,900), the largest of the three grants, with the strength of the Korean production team’s track record cited as a deciding factor in its selection. Popular on Variety Jakrawal Nilthamrong directs “Rhizome,” produced with Thailand carrying majority status while Korea, France, Laos and Singapore hold minority roles. Chatchai Chaiyon, Samavee Pummuang, Kim Hyejin, Yohann Cornu, Mattie Do and Panuksmi Hardjowirogo produce. The film centers on the wartime history shared across Asia and received KRW40 million ($28,600). Boo Junfeng directs “Trinity,” led by Taiwan, France and Singapore as majority partners, joined by eight minority partner countries: Poland, Greece, Germany, Japan, Brazil, Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines. Raymond Phathanavirangoon, Aileen Li, Sophie Erbs, Huang Junxiang, Boo Junfeng, Danny Yong, Takafumi Yuki, Mariusz Włodarski, Marta Gmosińska, Giorgos Karnavas, Danae Spathara, Jonas Katzenstein, Maximilian Leo, Eric Shih, Samuel Sagan, Mayra Faour Auad, Gabrielle Auad, Ilda Santiago, Yulia Evina Bhara, Oh Jungwan, Anita Tung, Bradley Liew, Bianca Balbuena and Stefano Centini produce. The film turns on a theme rooted in religion. The film also received KRW40 million ($28,600). Established in 2025, the Co-Production Support Fund was created to spur cross-border productions involving Korea. It supports long-form narrative features and animated theatrical releases structured as formal co-production pacts with Korea, requiring projects to have financed 60% or more of net production costs. Total funding rose to KRW140 million ($100,000) this year from KRW65 million ($46,400) in 2025, while the minimum guaranteed recipient count grew from one project to at least two. ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim said, “It is encouraging to see support for co-productions expanding since the launch of the Co-Production Support Fund last year, including the resumption of the Korean Film Council’s international co-production support program. The three projects have already made substantial progress in co-production and financing through collaboration with numerous international partners,” adding, “Now that these projects are close to bearing fruit, I hope this support – modest though it may be – will help put the final piece of the puzzle in place and bring each film to successful completion.” The ACF also runs a Script Development Fund, Post-Production Fund and Asian Network of Documentary (AND) Fund, connecting supported projects to distribution and industry access through BIFF and the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) programs. The 2026 ACFM runs Oct. 10-13 at Exhibition Center 2, BEXCO in Busan, alongside the 31st Busan International Film Festival, running Oct. 6-15. title: Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation
full_text: Aug 14, 2026 12:16am PT Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Nigel Farage Documentary ‘Where Does the Money Come From?’ Set at U.K. Broadcaster 5 as Parliamentary Standards Watchdog Reopens Finance Probe 38 minutes ago Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund 2 hours ago Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation 3 hours ago See All Yash Raj Films Bollywood star Rani Mukerji has been awarded an Honorary Doctor of Letters by Australia’s La Trobe University for three decades of work in Indian cinema and her contributions off screen, the university said. She is the second Indian film figure to receive the distinction, after superstar Shah Rukh Khan’s honor in 2019. “Receiving this honorary doctorate from La Trobe University is one of the most humbling moments of my life,” Mukerji said. “For someone who has always believed that films can change hearts before they change minds, this recognition means more than I can possibly express.” Related Stories ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery Khan’s doctorate marked his charitable work and standing in Indian film, and came with a Ph.D. scholarship set up in his name at the university. Mukerji’s own citation draws on similar ground: her screen career and the causes she has backed alongside it. Popular on Variety Mukerji said her film choices have always come down to what moved her personally first – stories that needed telling, that could inspire and empower. Every artist, she said, carries a responsibility beyond performance. “We quietly become ambassadors of our culture,” she said. On the impact of her work, she said, “If my films have helped even one person understand India and its women a little better… If they have encouraged dialogue… If they have created empathy… Then I feel I have fulfilled a responsibility far greater than simply being an actor.” Mukerji was separately honored with a special citation for acting excellence by the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne (IFFM), which cited her three decades of memorable roles and the international reach of her work. This year’s IFFM, running Aug. 13-23, gathers Indian filmmakers and films from around the country as part of its wider program. Her filmography includes “Black,” “Hum Tum,” “Yuva,” “Bunty Aur Babli,” “No One Killed Jessica,” “Hichki,” the “Mardaani” franchise and “Mrs. Chatterjee vs Norway.” On the IFFM honor, Mukerji said, “When I entered the Indian film industry as a young girl, I never imagined that one day my films and the characters that I have been fortunate enough to play, would take me across oceans and that people in a beautiful country like Australia would embrace me with so much warmth. Entertaining people across the world with my cinema is the greatest gift this profession has given me. Australia has always welcomed me & Indian cinema with open arms. It has become a place where cultures meet through storytelling, where films remind us that emotions don’t need passports and where love, laughter and hope speak a language we all understand.” Mukerji said that the real story of a performance begins only once it reaches an audience, not when it’s shot in front of a camera. “To know that for three decades my films, my characters and my voice have traveled so far from home and still found a place in your lives is incredibly humbling,” she said. “I’ve been fortunate to play women who laughed loudly, loved deeply, fought fearlessly and never stopped believing in themselves. In many ways, every character has changed me a little. They’ve made me a better actor, but more importantly, they’ve made me a better human being.” Meta Suspends AI Image Feature After Days of Backlash Meta AI Can Now Use Your Instagram Photos Without Consent. title: COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 14, 2026 12:00am PT COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Fukada Koji, Jakrawal Nilthamrong, Boo Junfeng Films Win Busan Co-Production Fund 2 hours ago Rani Mukerji Receives La Trobe Honorary Doctorate, Wins IFFM Special Citation 3 hours ago COL AI Studios Launches to Expand Group’s Global Distribution Network (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago See All COL Group COL Group has launched COL AI Studios, a new entertainment vertical designed to help platforms, studios and brands develop, test and scale content beyond traditional licensing deals. The studio builds on a distribution network that now counts over 5,000 live-action titles, up from a base of just over 1,000 when the network first launched, with content sourced from the United States, Europe, Southeast Asia and China. COL AI Studios adds a development layer that can move proven IP and original concepts into animation, short-form and long-form series, advertising, branded entertainment and live action. Related Stories 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ The launch comes as generative production tools make content creation faster and more accessible, a shift that has also driven a surge in programming built mainly for speed and volume. COL AI Studios is positioning itself differently, pairing established creative teams, commercially tested IP and audience data with what it calls responsible AI, aiming for stronger storytelling and franchise longevity rather than sheer output. Popular on Variety The company frames AI as one production method among several rather than a finished product, arguing it can help creators and partners test ideas and gauge audience response before greenlighting bigger-budget productions. COL Group’s library of more than 5,000 titles sits at the center of the model, built in part on thousands of commercially proven microdrama titles and backed by a roster exceeding 500 creative and production personnel – among them writers, directors, producers, editors and artists – based in Los Angeles, China and Southeast Asia. The company’s existing studio operations have already delivered more than 300 AI productions. For partners, the new studio widens the path for IP development, running from licensing and localization through animation, AI-powered production, branded entertainment and potentially premium live action. COL AI Studios is also pushing into branded AI entertainment, working with commercial partners to tap into the company’s creative and production network. Some early projects have already scaled into franchises. “Love Missions Across the Galaxy” has grown into a three-season franchise with localized versions in more than 10 languages, reaching number one in five overseas language markets. Several other AI-native titles are moving toward live-action development. Timothy Oh, general manager of COL Group International, said, “AI is ultimately another way of delivering a story. It can help creators and platforms understand how a concept performs before making the larger commitment required for live action. But greater access to these tools does not automatically lead to better entertainment, so storytelling, creative direction and responsible use of the technology still have to come first.” The company says protecting original IP and respecting creators remain central to how it applies the technology, positioning AI as a tool to strengthen development rather than replace the people driving it. Ray Tong, CEO of COL Group, said, “In China, AI-powered content is increasingly becoming part of mainstream storytelling, and we have had the opportunity to learn from that evolution first-hand. We now want to bring that experience to international platforms and brands, while recognizing that different markets will have different levels of receptiveness.” Meta AI Can Now Use Your Instagram Photos Without Consent. title: ‘The Ones With the Tempered Flowers’ Will Document a Woman Studying “Her Body’s Relationship to Self and Society” in Tanzania
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 13, 2026 11:59pm 'The Ones With the Tempered Flowers' Courtesy of Locarno Open Doors Tanzania-born director Neema Ngelime is working on her feature documentary debut. And the essayistic project has a title with poetic vibes: The Ones With the Tempered Flowers . It was among the works-in-progress presented at the 2026 edition of Open Doors , the Locarno Film Festival ‘s co-production platform and talent development program for filmmakers from equity-seeking communities and regions where artistic expression is at risk. The Tanzania-Kenya co-production is being produced by Ivy Kiru. The filmmaker has so far made shorts, namely A Country In A Corner , Hooyo, Why Here and An Ode to A Time I Loved Bread . At the end of the Locarno Open Doors program, her new project won the Sørfond Award and the ARTEKino International Award . Related Stories Movies China's $300M Sleeper Hit 'Dear You' Unveils U.S. Trailer Ahead of September Release TV Gerhard Zeiler to Receive 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award THR has compiled highlights about the movie and insight from Ngelime about The Ones With the Tempered Flowers and the themes it explores. Synopsis For Neema, being a woman has always meant a script: school, marriage, babies. When a doctor tells filmmaker Neema that having children might be hard, she doesn’t expect it to confuse her. Those expectations wound her. Raised in a multi-religious home, her identity was forged by questions of what is haram and what would please Jesus. All Neema cared about was which hell she’d end up in. To her, the older women in her family are a mystery beyond work and family. Their lives feel prophetic to her own. She and her sister try to rewrite their scripts through tarot. Her father taught her that anything is possible. Now he reminds her of her fate. She stages performances with her family, reenacting fragments of their lives. They believe these are fictions. But they’re memories, repurposed, hidden truths surfacing through play. This is the story of a woman studying her body’s relationship to self, society, and the political weight placed on women’s bodies in Tanzania, challenging duty masked as love. Director’s note Growing up felt like watching the women I loved fade into mysteries. Now, with fibroids, a condition society pins on “unused” womanhood, I fear becoming a mystery too, lost to the weight of expectations. The women in my life shaped me deeply, yet I knew little about who they were before becoming mothers or wives. This erasure fills me with grief. Through this film, I channel that grief, exploring how families shape dreams, identity and autonomy. I look inward and center myself and my family to reflect on my past and imagine my future. The film relies on metaphor to reflect the absurdity of how womanhood is confined. It captures the reality of existing in a patriarchal world, where women are bound by timed beauty and defined by their choice to give birth. While rooted in the experiences of young African women, it speaks to a universal audience, inviting viewers to reflect on their own relationships with identity, self-expression and societal constructs. What was the inspiration for you, personal or otherwise, to want to make this film? The film itself starts from a personal point of view, from my confronting and going through an existential crisis because of my diagnosis. When I got my diagnosis, I was angry that I found out so late in life that this could happen, and angry at how it could happen. I was also angry at how little interest there is in understanding women’s bodies. Out of that, the film became about someone wanting to find answers. So in a way, this was my way of creating a space for people going through what I’m going through, a space to talk. But mostly, it was a way to have these conversations with the people close to us, i.e. our families. Making my small inquiries with the people I love, that is the inspiration. Can you share some thoughts on how universal the themes of the film are, and why people outside your home should see it? The universal themes are womanhood and its place in 21st-century society, identity, and curiosity as an act of care across generations. Do you know what the next step or focus for you and any collaborators on the film will be after Open Doors? We’re going back home with so much clarity, thanks to the guidance we’ve received. I’m going to continue my treatment, and the project will also participate in the Durban FilmMart in October, and the Sørfond pitching event in November THR

title: Busan Film Festival to Honor Its Founder Kim Dong-ho with Korean Cinema Award
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All August 13, 2026 10:30pm Kim Dong-ho in 'Walking in the Movies' Courtesy of the Cannes Film Festival For this year’s Korean Cinema Award, the Busan International Film Festival will be honoring one of its own — the event’s founding OG, in fact. Kim Dong-ho, who established BIFF in 1996 and ran the event for its first 14 years, will receive the prize at the festival’s opening ceremony on Oct. 6. The award goes annually to figures who have advanced Korean cinema’s standing in the world — and few, perhaps, are as worthy as the founder of the festival himself. When BIFF launched in 1996, Korean films were still routinely submitted to government censors for pre-screening before public exhibition. Kim refused to put the festival’s program through that process, a stand that established BIFF’s independence, won the trust of filmmakers across the region and helped turn a first-year event in a Korean port city into the leading cinema showcase in Asia . The festival became the meeting ground and incubator for the Korean directors who would sweep the world in the early and mid-2000s, contributing significantly to the broader Korean cultural wave that continues today. Related Stories Movies China's $300M Sleeper Hit 'Dear You' Unveils U.S. Trailer Ahead of September Release TV Gerhard Zeiler to Receive 2026 International Emmy Directorate Award Kim brought a rare but essential combination of skills to BIFF’s early days — a bureaucrat’s background but a cinephile’s instincts. He spent roughly three decades at what is now South Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, rising to vice minister. He also served as president of the state film body now known as the Korean Film Council, as well as founding president of the Seoul Arts Center. After stepping down as festival director in 2010, he stayed in the field as dean of Dankook University’s Graduate School of Cinematic Content, chairman of the Presidential Committee for Cultural Enrichment and, later, chairman of BIFF. He has sat on festival juries at Cannes — where he presided over the Un Certain Regard section — Rotterdam and Fukuoka. At age 85, Kim, quite improbably, began work on his first feature. His full-length directorial debut, the documentary Mr. Kim Goes to the Cinema , premiered as a special screening at BIFF’s 30th edition last year and opened in Korean theaters in February, when he was 88. Shot as the pandemic emptied theaters worldwide, the film follows him around the globe in conversation with filmmaker friends, including Bong Joon Ho, Park Chan-wook, Lee Chang-dong, Hirokazu Kore-eda, Tang Wei, Luc Besson and the Dardenne brothers about what purpose cinema now serves. He had previously directed a 2013 short, Jury , and was himself the subject of Walking in the Movies , a 2024 documentary that played Cannes Classics. “I feel deeply moved and humbled to be recognized by the very festival I helped establish and served for over 15 years,” Kim said in a statement released Thursday. The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs Oct. 6-15. Kim will be honored at an opening ceremony that also hands Michelle Yeoh the Asian Filmmaker of the Year award and Ann Hui the Chanel-backed Camellia Award, with Pachinko star Kim Minha hosting. “Even today, I attend more than ten film festivals each year to promote Korean cinema,” Kim added, “and I hope to continue this journey for as long as I can.” THR

title: Phoebe Bridgers Leads Delighted Fans Around the Rink at a Rollerskating Listening Party for ‘Lost Weekend’
full_text: Aug 13, 2026 9:28pm PT Phoebe Bridgers Leads Delighted Fans Around the Rink at a Rollerskating Listening Party for ‘Lost Weekend’ The beaming singer relished in taking slow songs out for a spin, as she made a surprise appearance at the YouTube-sponsored event, also doing a Q&A about an album she hasn't otherwise discussed publicly. By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Phoebe Bridgers Leads Delighted Fans Around the Rink at a Rollerskating Listening Party for ‘Lost Weekend’ 5 hours ago Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’ 1 day ago The Band Perry’s Family Feud Lights Up: Neil Perry Says He Was ‘Terminated’ From Sibling Trio, as Kimberly Perry’s Husband Stepped In to Make It a Marital Duo 2 days ago See All @linusandhiscamera Phoebe Bridgers tends to stand out in a crowd, and not just because of her celebrity or natural star quality, but because of the hair; other women around L.A. may go for the platinum blonde look, but not quite that platinum. So it was fairly easy to pick her out for the entirety of the 10 minutes or so she spent skating with her fans Tuesday night at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California. But she was easy to spot, in this instance, from head to toe, as she was the only skater on the floor in brightly strobing light-up skates… an equipment option that the Moonlight was not able to offer any of the couple hundred fans who joined her. At this very action-packed listening party for her. The beaming Bridgers had earned the right to wear skates that special; this was not her first rodeo, clearly, when it came to making dozens of laps around a rink and outpacing a crowd. Related Stories ‘Reacher’ Star Alan Ritchson Slams ‘F—ing Pedophiles’ in Politics: ‘I Would Get Those Epstein Files Out in Two Seconds … Bitch, Move’ 'Reacher' Spinoff 'Neagley' Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery As one fan commented on Reddit after the YouTube-sponsored event: “She was skating right with everyone, and if you could match her speed then you could say hello, but she is FAST so it may have been a bit difficult.” Popular on Variety Of all the albums that could be previewed with an evening out at an old-school roller rink, “Lost Weekend,” the singer’s long-awaited third solo album, would not jump out as the most obvious candidate… even if Bridgers is hell on wheels, as it turns out. The 16-track record has as many hushed passages as you’d expect from a Bridgers album, and it does not sound at all designed to inspire extended bouts of cardiovascular activity. And Bridgers did use the word “weird” in characterizing the juxtaposition when she spoke about her reasons for hosting the event there in a brief Q&A she did with fans at the event after the skating wound down. Yet, for her, it was an aspiration being realized. “I’ve had this idea forever” she said to the crowd of about 200 sitting on the rink’s floor. “I always thought it would be cool to do like a Grouper Moonlight night… You always kind of skate to ABBA or something. I thought it would be interesting to listen to sad and slow songs and skate.” Phoebe Bridgers skates at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera She’s had the same impulse at amusement parks, she pointed out. “I always thought about that at Six Flags,” she said saying that, while waiting in line for rides, she’d wished she could take the typical revved-up theme-park soundtrack and “catapult it somewhere” and replace it with music that was “30 bpm or something.” To her mind, slowcore and Tatsu might be the perfect fit. Anyway, Bridgers’ promotional campaign for “Lost Weekend” has been unusual enough that a rollerskating listening party almost — almost — doesn’t stand out as that unusual. ,The singer-songwriter first began teasing “Lost Weekend” a few months ago with a series of pop-up gigs in small towns and middle American cities, places like Roswell, New Mexico, before the album was announced or even widely known to be in production. WIth the moment of release finally at hand, her team booked planetariums across the country and even in Europe for Spotify-sponsored listening parties where fans could experience the album for the first time this week with trippy visuals, if sore necks — a way of getting “Lost” in space, sort of. (And no phones allowed, as with virtually every pre-release event for the record.) Another fairy unusual element of the promo campaign: no interviews. She hasn’t done a single one for “Lost Weekend,” so the roughly six minutes she spent answering fan questions at the Moonlight Rollerway may have constituted as much talking about the record as she plans to do, at least right away. Bridgers didn’t exactly talk anyone’s ear off in her quick, friendly response to the fan queries, but the answers still offered glimpses of insight as to where she’s coming from with this album and its attendant cycle of events and touring. One of the first hands that went up from the crowd was to ask whether she’d been inspired by any other artistic media while making the record. “Well, there’s a movie called ‘Lost Weekend’ that’s about alcoholics’ kind of fugue state,” she said, referencing the harrowing 1945 Billy Wilder drama that some of her younger fans might not know. “That probably goes well (with the album), unfortunately.” She hesitated while trying to think of another example, then did come up with a musical reference point. “Do you guys know ‘The Lemon of Pink’ by the Books?” (Not everyone did — the Books are not exactly a household name — but some murmured their assent for the 2003 album, which has a strong following as a seminal indie-oughts cult record.) Phoebe Bridgers does a Q&A with fans at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera Someone else wondered: Why the small-town pop-up tour? And what was her takeaway from what seemed like it might be an experiment? “I just wanted everything with this album to feel like it’s happening in real life,” she explained. “Like, I didn’t live through a time where I didn’t find out about something on the internet. Even cool pop-up shows and stuff, it was all kind of phone-based. So I just liked the idea of plastering a small town (with flyers)… It was so fun.” Her answer to the second part of the question: “The biggest takeaway was like, yeah, the internet’s not real. It’s all a fake,” she said, to laughter. Another question: How did she decide it was time to come back? — the unspoken assumption being that six years between albums counts as a lot, even if there was a monumental Boygenius album and tour in between that came to feel like a very viable separate career. “I mean, I didn’t love all parts of being away,” she said, with a chuckle, noting that while she knew she needed to pull away for a bit, it wasn’t necessarily a plan to wait this long. “I kept booking studio time and then putting it off… and booking studio time and putting it off, and putting it off… I really wanted to be making something,” she allowed, but the album was not yet ready to take shape. “So I just started going in and then taking six months off and then going (back). So this album took forever. Which is great!,” she added, harboring no regrets about leaving anyone in suspense. After those and a few other questions, it was time for her to sign the big stack of posters commemorating the event. Prior to the Q&A, meanwhile, Bridgers premiered a rough cut of the second video for the album, for the song “I Can’t Wait,” which she said was nearly done, except for some drone footage that was shot during this very event that will be folded in. Phoebe Bridgers signs posters for fans at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera There was a no-phones policy, but there were also no NDAs, so fans freely shared their experiences on Reddit and other forums after the event… including their impressions about Phoebe Bridgers being as good at skating as at music. “I ate shit 3 times out there and got a sore ass today,” wrote one fan. “It was even more embarrassing because she was shredding around the rink.” Others spoke of approaching Bo Burnham or Bridgers’ mother, Jamie Bridgers, for off-rink convos. But when it came to meeting the star attraction, some found her intimidating, despite her best efforts to be a fairly unassuming skatergrl. Some agonized afterward about not having found the right words when they made it to the front of the signing line. One spoke of becoming tongue-tied, but “I was towards the end of the line and it had been almost 2 hours at that point. She probably did appreciate our efficiency lol!!” Another wrote, “I just said ‘Yo this album fucking rips,’ and she laughed and said thanks.” One person who admitted being unable to do anything but blurt out their name said that as they left the signing table, Bridgers politely called out, “It was nice to meet you.” Phoebe Bridgers skates at the Moonlight Rollerway in Glendale, California during a YouTube release party for ‘Lost Weekend.’ @linusandhiscamera What will she do for an encore? That’s obvious: do sold-out two- and three-nighters at the nation’s biggest arenas, like the three-night stand she has upcoming at the Intuit Dome Oct. 30-31 and Nov. 1. Between now and then, there is much parsing of the 16-track album’s rich content to be done, with millions of words of formal and informal think-pieces to come. (Read Variety ‘s own take on the album here .) While fans who didn’t make it to the Moonlight Rollerway may have a lingering case of FOMO, it may still be possible to replicate the feel that Bridgers was going for, as she’s longed to marry slow sounds with frenetic action. You could go to Magic Mountain and do X2 while listening to “Lost Weekend” on earbuds; we can now be certain the author would approve. title: Alexa Nikolas Wins Key Ruling In Defamation Case Against Bryan Freedman Over Smear Claims
full_text: Skip to main content By Winston Cho Plus Icon Winston Cho View All August 13, 2026 7:43pm Attorney Bryan Freedman has represented many controversial Hollywood figures. CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP/Getty Images Logo text Months after a resolution to the sprawling legal battle over the filming of It Ends With Us , Hollywood power lawyer Bryan Freedman is still dealing with fallout from the case. Zoey 101 alum Alexa Nikolas won a key ruling on Wednesday in a defamation lawsuit against Freedman, with a court finding that she’s established a probability of prevailing on defamation claims accusing him and those in his orbit of marshaling a smear campaign against her. Nikolas, founder of advocacy organization Eat Predators, has a long and contentious history with Freedman, who had represented her ex-husband Michael Milosh when she sued the musician for sexual abuse. She had organized protests outside of his offices in 2022 after discovering that he had also been accused of sexual assault in a case that resulted in a no-fault settlement in 1991. Around the time of these protests, a smear site that aimed to undermine her activism — including through assertions that her current husband was a predator — popped up about her. Nikolas didn’t connect Freedman to the site until Lively sued It Ends With Us director Justin Baldoni and his production company Wayfarer. The thrust of Lively’s lawsuit focused on alleged sexual harassment on the set of the film, but it also accused Baldoni and his public relations team — led by top crisis publicist Melissa Nathan and digital fixer Jed Wallace — of spawning a smear machine that threatened her reputation. This led to sister lawsuits, including one from publicist Stephanie Jones, who claimed that Nathan and Wallace have long engaged in creating smear sites targeting women. That gave Nikolas the ammunition to file a lawsuit, which points to alleged data identifying Freedman as involved in the generation of some of the sites. In Wednesday’s ruling, Los Angeles Superior Court judge Michael Whitaker rebuffed Freedman’s bid to dismiss the case. He concluded that Nikolas has produced enough evidence to potentially prove the alleged campaign was defamatory. Among the findings: Nikolas sufficiently demonstrated a probability of proving the allegedly defamatory statements were untrue. This includes a claim on a second smear site about her that she partnered with former California senator Joe Dunn to push others into making false accusations of sexual assault. Whitaker also pointed to court records across multiple cases in which several plaintiffs describe a “similar modus operandi and common website traffic optimization tactics.” Freedman had argued that Nikolas can’t prove the assertions advanced in the sites were false and that some were simply statements of opinion, which can’t give rise to a defamation claim. On this front, the court said that the allegations in the site “all imply provably false assertions of fact” that Nikolas is “either a criminal who has committed criminal acts, or she is not.” Multiple smear sites identified in the case between Jones and Baldoni appear to have evidence of common authorship, including Alexanikolas.net, which claimed she extorted multiple ex-boyfriends by threatening them with manufacturing sexual abuse claims, among other things. In Jones’ case, a cybersecurity expert submitted an expert report indicating that those who created the site about Nikolas may have also created ones about Amanda Ghost, who’s engaged in a defamation battle against Rebel Wilson. “There is a tangled web of connections between these sites and numerous others in addition to that authored about plaintiff,” Whitaker wrote, noting a “conspiracy to smear various individuals” who had adversarial connections to Freedman’s clients. That not only suggests a motive, the court found, but also indicates that the lawyer may have been “involved in directing or otherwise effectuating all of those alleged smear campaigns.” Earlier this year, Wilson’s crisis public relations team — comprised of Nathan and Wallace — was heard discussing plans to create anonymous sites that accused Ghost of sex trafficking as part of an alleged smear campaign solicited by the actress against The Deb producer. In a recording obtained by The Hollywood Reporter, Wallace instructed Nathan to assert without evidence that Ghost is a “madame” whose work involves procuring young women for wealthy and powerful men. “We can’t just do, like, oh, she’s a bitch, she sucks,” Wallace says in the recording. “It’s, like, it’s got to be really, really heavy and connected to something that heavy.” At one point in the conversation, Wallace referenced the involvement of Freedman, Wilson’s then-counsel in the case. Freedman and Nathan didn’t respond to requests for comment, though they’ve previously denied involvement in the creation of the smear sites. THR
